families.name: Fresh
families.blurb: Unripened, eaten within days. Acid or a little rennet sets the curd; nothing lives on the outside.

families.name: Bloomy-rind
families.blurb: A white mold coat ripens the paste from the rind inwards, so the edge softens before the center.

families.name: Washed-rind
families.blurb: Brine or a brine-and-culture wash on the outside every few days. Orange, tacky, and louder than it tastes.

families.name: Blue
families.blurb: Blue mold introduced to the curd, then air let in by piercing. Salt carries the whole balance.

families.name: Semi-hard
families.blurb: Pressed, salted and aged a few months. The broad middle of the trade and the hardest family to sell badly.

families.name: Hard / alpine
families.blurb: Cooked curd, heavily pressed, aged long. Made large because it was made to keep a valley through winter.

families.name: Pasta filata
families.blurb: Curd heated and stretched until it ropes. Texture is decided in thirty seconds of pulling.

families.name: Natural-rind
families.blurb: No wash, no mold coat: the rind is whatever the cave grows on it, brushed and turned.

styles.name: Lactic curd fresh
styles.description: Set slowly with very little rennet, drained in cloth and salted lightly. Tastes of the milk it was made from and almost nothing else.
styles.lookFor: Clean acidity with no bitterness at the back. A weeping, slumped tub means it was drained hot.

styles.name: Drained goat log
styles.description: A hand-ladled log, sometimes rolled in ash, that firms and sharpens across a fortnight. Sold at three ages by shops that know their customers.
styles.lookFor: A fine wrinkle starting at the ends. Slick, wet skin means it sat in its own moisture.

styles.name: Whey ricotta-style
styles.description: Recooked from the whey of a harder make, so it exists because something else was made first. Sweet, grainy and very perishable.
styles.lookFor: Loose grain that holds its shape on a spoon. Rubbery means it was cooked too hard.

styles.name: Bloomy disc
styles.description: The classic white-coated disc: mold ripens it from the outside in, so a young one has a chalky line down the middle and an old one has none.
styles.lookFor: An even, close coat with no gray. Ammonia on the nose means it is past, not ripe.

styles.name: Triple-cream round
styles.description: Cream added back to the milk before setting. Rich enough that most people eat a third of what they intended to.
styles.lookFor: A paste that slumps but does not run. A sunken top means the rind collapsed early.

styles.name: Ash-lined goat pyramid
styles.description: A truncated pyramid dusted with ash before the mold takes, which slows the rind and lets the paste catch up.
styles.lookFor: Gray-blue bloom over the ash, even on the corners. Cracked corners mean it dried unevenly.

styles.name: Washed-rind square
styles.description: Washed two or three times a week until the rind turns orange and tacky. Smells far more assertive than it tastes.
styles.lookFor: A supple, slightly sticky rind. A dry, cracked rind means the washing stopped early.

styles.name: Brine-washed wheel
styles.description: A larger washed format that holds its shape for months. The paste goes translucent at the edge as it ages.
styles.lookFor: Even color under the rind. A dark band more than a few millimeters deep means it was held too warm.

styles.name: Washed-rind sheep tomme
styles.description: Sheep milk under a washed rind: fattier paste, so the wash reads as savory rather than barnyard.
styles.lookFor: A close, fine paste with no mechanical openings. Pinholes mean gas where none should be.

styles.name: Natural-rind blue
styles.description: Pierced twice to let air to the mold, then left to grow its own rind. The blue runs in seams rather than spots.
styles.lookFor: Veining that follows the piercing lines. Gray-brown mush at the veins means it over-ripened.

styles.name: Sheep's-milk blue
styles.description: Higher fat and higher salt than a cow blue, which is why it reads sweet before it reads sharp.
styles.lookFor: White paste, not yellow, with a clean salt finish. Bitterness usually means young milk and old salt.

styles.name: Creamy blue log
styles.description: A soft blue made in a small format so it ripens fast. Spreadable at the edge by six weeks.
styles.lookFor: A soft edge and a firmer center. Uniformly runny means it has gone.

styles.name: Mountain tomme
styles.description: The everyday wheel of a mountain make: pressed, brined and turned, eaten young by the people who made it.
styles.lookFor: A dry, dusty gray rind and an elastic paste. A greasy rind means it was wrapped too soon.

styles.name: Farmhouse cloth-bound
styles.description: Bound in cloth and larded, so the rind breathes and the paste dries slowly. Ages into something brothy rather than sharp.
styles.lookFor: Cloth still bonded to the rind. Lifting cloth means moisture got underneath.

styles.name: Goat tomme
styles.description: A pressed goat wheel, which is rarer than it should be: most goat milk goes to fresh formats because it pays sooner.
styles.lookFor: Bright white paste with a firm break. Yellowing under the rind means oxidation.

styles.name: Brined sheep wheel
styles.description: Held in brine through its aging rather than salted dry, which keeps the paste close and the flavor direct.
styles.lookFor: Firm, close paste with no rind to speak of. Crumbling at the edge means the brine was too strong.

styles.name: Alpine eye wheel
styles.description: Cooked curd pressed into a large wheel; a second fermentation opens round eyes as it warms in the cellar.
styles.lookFor: Round, shiny eyes and a slight sweetness. Splits and cracks mean the eyes opened too fast.

styles.name: Alpine grating wheel
styles.description: The long-aged end of the family. Dry enough to grate, with the crystals that come of protein breaking down over years.
styles.lookFor: Crunch that dissolves, not grit that stays. A soapy finish means it was aged damp.

styles.name: Aged sheep grating
styles.description: A hard sheep wheel made to be grated over food rather than eaten in a wedge. Salt-forward by design.
styles.lookFor: A clean, even break. Ammonia at the rind means it was held too long in plastic.

styles.name: Fresh stretched curd
styles.description: Curd ripened to the right acidity, then stretched in hot water and torn into balls. The texture is decided in half a minute.
styles.lookFor: A thin skin that tears to layers, and milky liquid when cut. Squeaky and tight means it was stretched too cold.

styles.name: Aged stretched wheel
styles.description: The same stretch, then shaped, brined and hung to dry for months. Layers stay visible in the paste.
styles.lookFor: Visible grain when you break it along the stretch. A rubbery, uniform paste means it was over-worked.

styles.name: Smoked braided curd
styles.description: Braided while warm and cold-smoked. A format built for a market stall rather than a cellar.
styles.lookFor: Smoke on the outside only, in a thin band. Smoke all the way through means heat, not time.

styles.name: Cloth-bound territorial
styles.description: The long-aged crumbling style: pressed hard, cloth-bound, and left until the paste breaks rather than bends.
styles.lookFor: A break that flakes along a plane. Bendy paste at eighteen months means it was pressed light.

styles.name: Leaf-wrapped natural rind
styles.description: Wrapped in leaves for the cellar, which is a handling decision that became a flavor one.
styles.lookFor: Leaves still pliable and bonded. Dry, lifting leaves mean the cellar ran dry.

styles.name: Cave-aged natural tomme
styles.description: Brushed and turned in a cave, with whatever the cave grows allowed to form the rind. No two batches match.
styles.lookFor: A mottled gray rind with no bald patches. Orange slime means it turned into a washed rind by accident.
